extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of medieval mathematics, natural philosophy, music theory, optics, and meteorology
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from a medieval scientific treatise covering methods of geometric demonstration (composition/resolution), identification of fallacies in proofs, arithmetic and proportion problems, practical music-teaching methods, optics for horologia, and signs for weather and medical prognosis. The page is prescriptive/horticultural in parts (how to demonstrate, how to teach, how to read signs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of compositio/resolutio method in geometric demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Compofita methodus, quam proposuimus in laterum heptagoni demonstratione; initium sumit. (The method of composition and resolution is taken as the method for demonstrating geometrical problems, e.g., the heptagon.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin demonstrations by composition (constructing the figure/target) and follow by resolutio (resolving back to known principles). Be careful: errors occur if the worker is not fully attentive to steps. Examples and extended expositions follow in the text showing how composed constructions must be linked to demonstrable ratios and known elements; anti-pattern: adopting a composed assumption that lacks a resolutive demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid paralogisms (fallacies) in demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: In universum paralogismi fiunt vel cum assumitur aliquid in constructione problematis quo non utimur in demonstratione, vel cum utimur principio non vero, sed verisimili, vel cum assumimus non demonstrata pro demonstratis, vel pro tangunt in remotis sensu, ut corporibus & diversi generis quantitatibus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not: (1) assume during problem-construction something that is not actually used in the demonstration; (2) rely on principles that are not true but only plausible; (3) treat undemonstrated things as if they were demonstrated; (4) conflate distinct kinds (e.g., corporeal quantities and abstract magnitudes) or take remote senses as equivalent. The text gives geometric examples (circle-center constructions) showing how such mistakes lead to false conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting paralogisms by identifying false experiments or defects in middle terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicio autem paralogismi est falsiexperimentum in conclusione vel mediis; aut deprehensio alicuius defectus ex his dictis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sign that a demonstration is paralogistic (fallacious) is that some experiment asserted as evidence is false within the conclusion or middle terms, or that some defect can be traced to the stated assumptions. Use detection by checking middle terms and the experimental claims; the text presents examples where geometrical 'experiments' (constructions) mask invalid inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition must have a known end and ratio of quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: In compositione notus necesse est finis & rationem nostram esse illarum (in genere diversarum quantitatum finem & rationem nostram esse illarum oportet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing a construction or solving by composition, one must know the intended terminus (end) and the ratios/relations among the involved quantities. Without known proportions the composition cannot be reliably resolved. The discussion of the impossibility of squaring the circle illustrates that lacking a demonstrable relation (e.g., rational proportion of circumference to diameter) prevents legitimate composition-based solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept as knowledge what lacks demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Cüm ad certam notiosnem non deveniat absque demonstrationis auxilio, non licet illam percipere ante demonstrationem. (One must not claim to know a thing until it has been demonstrated.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists on demonstration as the standard of knowledge: apparent results (even if attractive or traditional) must be accompanied by demonstration. Anti-pattern: claiming an effect or proportion 'can be known' merely by authority or plausible construction without proof (examples include attempted squarings or Archimedean constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: On proportions and maximal/minimal proportion problems: rely on explicit arithmetic/algorithmic demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations of maximal or special proportional relations (e.g., 'proportio dupli tertiae quantitatis ad aggregatum primae & quartae') require explicit arithmetic demonstration and careful accounting of terms; such demonstrations can be difficult and need concrete algorithmic steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting inequalities or maximality among proportions, provide stepwise arithmetic verification (the text works through long number manipulations to establish which ratio is larger). Anti-pattern: asserting comparative magnitude of complex proportions without exhibiting the numeric or algebraic steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music-teaching methods for transferring syllables to notes (three methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fit autem haec translatio tribus modis. Primus est ut quis diapente; diapafon; diateffaron ...; Secundus modus est vt mente concipias quocunque spatium; ac linea, quae vox & quanta esse debeat... Tertius omnium optimus est ut imaginatione & voce quidem notas, & vocum magnitudinem retineas, lingua vero syllabam subiectam proferas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three prescribed methods to teach rendering words under musical notes: (1) transpose by established interval relations (diapente, diapason, diatessaron) and map intermediate consonances so syllables fall under note magnitudes — easier but limited; (2) mentally conceive the spatial/line mapping of voice to quantity so syllables are voiced according to position — better than first when semitones occur; (3) best (but hardest): memorize notes and voice-magnitudes by imagination and sing syllables beneath sustained notes, using a helper who sings notes while the learner speaks syllables; practice routines: start with longer durations, ascend/ descend, practice in diapason/diapente/diatessaron, then transfer to normal tempo. The text offers practical sequences and warns about difficulties (third is most effective but most difficult).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of optical instruments (horologia) and meridian alignment for timekeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: Optica disciplina, cuius subtilissimum inventum est horologiorum; quae umbris horas edocent ... instrumento iuxta lineas meridianas situm ad horam ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For constructing shadow-based clocks (horologia), align the instrument to the meridian and mark shadow divisions on planes described by right/left lines; correct placement and knowledge of meridian lines ensure hourly indication. The text indicates optical theory as 'medium' among mathematical arts for such devices and sketches constructional aims; anti-pattern: building without meridian orientation or without careful division of shadow spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological signs and their interpretation (classification and cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aeris conformationes duabus constant differentiis, quarum altera in frigido & calido; reliqua verò circa humidum & siccum versatur. Hoc in genere quinque sunt species: serenum, ventosum, nubes, imbres, grando; seu horrida tempestas. Ventorum signa: nubecula circa lunam, rubes nubes ad solis occasum, vexilla in turrium culminibus moventur, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify air by hot/cold and moist/dry, and recognize five weather types. Use signs to forecast: e.g., small clouds around the moon predict winds; red clouds at moonrise or sunset signal forthcoming winds; specific animal and plant behaviors (cattle licking hooves, birds' movements, certain insects) and cloud colors indicate rain or storms. However, the author cautions some signs are fallacious and context-dependent: some signs are deceptive, and multiple indicators should be considered. The text gives many concrete signs and notes when they are more or less reliable (season, locality, duration of calm, preceding phenomena).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use meteorological signs with medical prognostication but beware of fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Per has constitutiones temporum praecognoscere rerum & morborum genera potest; Hippocrates & Aristotle treat these signs with subtlety. Sed signum fallax est; nam aliquae notiones apparent ut deliquia, sed falsae sunt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply weather/air-constitution signs to predict human health trends (hot/dry airs yield certain fevers, etc.), but do so cautiously: some signs are reliable predictors of epidemics or fevers (as noted by Hippocrates), whereas others are misleading. The text recommends selecting the most evident and useful signs and warns against over-reliance on single or poetic 'signs' (e.g., Virgil) without empirical corroboration.
